issues.failure_explanation: The mask $\binom{n}{i}$ for $i=0,\ldots,n$ sums to $2^n\neq 1$ and does not reproduce constants, so the resulting scheme cannot be convergent or generate splines. Applying the mask in (2.1) for $n=1$ gives $v^{k+1}_{2i+1}=v^k_i$, contradicting the explicit rule (2.2) which states $v^{k+1}_{2i+1}=\tfrac12(v^k_i+v^k_{i+1})$. The correct degree-$n$ B-spline mask (recoverable from the stated $n=1,2$ rules) is $\frac{1}{2^n}\binom{n+1}{i}$ with appropriate index shifts.

failure_location.quote: The subdivision scheme based on the refinement operator $S_n$ with the mask $\binom{n}{i}, i=0,\ldots n$, is convergent for any $n\in\N$ and generates limit curves which are splines with integer knots, of degree $n$ with continuous derivatives up to order $n-1$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the mask formula $\binom{n}{i}$ with the correct degree-$n$ B-spline mask $\frac{1}{2^n}\binom{n+1}{i}$ (with appropriate indexing), consistent with the stated $n=1$ and $n=2$ refinement rules.
issues.overall_effect: The general claim that the stated mask generates spline curves is false; the specific explicit rules for $n=1$ and $n=2$ remain correct.
issues.title: B-spline subdivision mask formula is incorrect
issues.why_classification: A one-line formula correction restores the claim; the explicit examples and all downstream results are already correct and unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: A map $A_\omega \colon \Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega$ is called a binary average (or, for short, average) in $X$ if it satisfies:
It is easy to verify that if the metric $d$ is continuous as a function of its arguments, then the binary Fr\'echet mean satisfies all the requirements of Definition~\ref{def:average}.

issues.failure_explanation: Definition 3.1 requires $A_\omega$ to be a well-defined map $\Omega\times\Omega\to\Omega$. The argmin of the Fréchet functional need not be unique (e.g., in an equilateral three-point metric space at $\omega=1/2$ both endpoints minimise). Additionally, the boundedness condition (item 5) can fail: from optimality one obtains only $d(x,A_\omega(x,y))\le\sqrt{\omega/(1-\omega)}\,d(x,y)$, which exceeds $d(x,y)$ for $\omega>1/2$. The stated continuity hypothesis on $d$ is vacuous (every metric is continuous in its arguments).

failure_location.quote: It is easy to verify that if the metric $d$ is continuous as a function of its arguments, then the binary Fr\'echet mean satisfies all the requirements of Definition~\ref{def:average}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the example to metric spaces where the Fréchet mean is unique and satisfies all five properties (e.g., complete simply connected non-positively curved geodesic spaces), or specify a canonical selection rule and verify the properties under explicit hypotheses.
issues.overall_effect: The claim that the binary Fréchet mean is always a valid average per Definition 3.1 is false; other averages used in the paper (metric average on compact sets, Wasserstein geodesic, Hermite Bézier average) are unaffected.
issues.title: Binary Fréchet mean is not a well-defined average in general metric spaces
issues.why_classification: Adding standard geometric hypotheses (unique geodesicity or non-positive curvature) restores the example, but the current blanket claim for arbitrary metric spaces is materially false and requires more than a one-line fix.

Hence $[t_{2j}^{k+1},t_{2j+2}^{k+1})$ generally crosses $t_{j+1}^k$ (as happens for the dual parameterization), so the claimed containment fails. issues.failure_explanation: The $L$-power proximity (the remark after Definition 6.1) gives error $E\eta^{j+1}$ at block index $j=\ell/L-1$, i.e., $E\eta^{\ell/L}$. The proof writes $E\eta^{\ell-L+1}$, which for $L>1$ is strictly smaller than the true proximity error $E\eta^{\ell/L}$ and does not follow from the hypothesis. The same wrong exponent appears in Theorem 6.4's proof in the divided-difference bound $2\cdot2^{\ell}E\eta^{\ell-L_1+1}$ (which also contains a factor-of-$\eta$ algebra slip equated to $\frac{2E}{\eta^{L_1}}(2\eta)^{\ell}$).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace $\eta^{\ell-L+1}$ with $\eta^{\ell/L}$ in (6.3) and the analogous divided-difference bound in Theorem 6.4's proof, and redo the unrolled sums; the summability conclusion of Theorem 6.2 is preserved.
issues.overall_effect: The key recursions in the proofs of Theorems 6.2 and 6.4 are derived from an incorrect bound. For Theorem 6.2 the summability conclusion survives with corrected exponents. For Theorem 6.4 the corrected exponent $\eta^{\ell/L_1}$ yields rate $2\eta^{1/L_1}$ which can exceed 1 (see ISSUE-007).
issues.title: Wrong exponent on η in the second-type proximity error bounds

issues.failure_explanation: The proof explicitly invokes the D-S property of $S_1$ to bound $d(S_1^{\ell+1}(\PP)_{2j},S_1^{\ell}(\PP)_{j})$, but no D-S hypothesis appears in the theorem. The theorem is false without it: taking $\Omega=\R$ with the arithmetic average, $S_2(\PP)_{2j}=p_j+1$, $S_2(\PP)_{2j+1}=\tfrac12(p_j+p_{j+1})+1$ is contractive ($\mu=\tfrac12$, $L=1$) and trivially in proximity with $S_1=S_2$, yet $S_2^k(\PP)_{2^kj}=p_j+k$ diverges. The remark after the theorem wrongly asserts that D-S is unnecessary.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis that $S_1$ is D-S in $\D$ to Theorem 6.2 (and consequently to Theorem 6.4), and correct the remark to acknowledge the requirement.
issues.overall_effect: The convergence claim of Theorem 6.2 is false as stated (and the convergence half of Theorem 6.4 inherits the defect). The remark claiming D-S is not needed is also false. Applications where the scheme is D-S (e.g., Theorem 6.12) are unaffected.
issues.title: Theorem 6.2 uses displacement-safety of S₁ without assuming it
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard local condition (D-S) preserves the convergence conclusion and the proof architecture for D-S schemes; the scope reduction is limited and the result remains recognizably comparable.

issues.failure_explanation: The proximity of order $m=1$ for $S_1^{L_1}$ to $S_2^{L_1}$ gives error $E\eta^{j+1}$ at block index $j$. Divided-difference normalisation introduces a factor $2^{\ell}=2^{(j+1)L_1}$, so the effective rate is $2^{L_1}\eta$ per block, equivalently $2\eta^{1/L_1}$ per refinement. The hypothesis $\eta<(1/2)^m=1/2$ guarantees $2\eta<1$ (rate decays) only when $L_1=1$. For $L_1\ge 2$ and $\eta$ near $1/2$ one has $2\eta^{1/L_1}>1$, so the divided differences diverge and the limit is not $C^1$. The proof's rate $\alpha=\max\{2\eta,\mu_1\}<1$ is an artefact of the wrong exponent (ISSUE-005); with the correct exponent the rate is $\max\{2\eta^{1/L_1},\mu_1\}$, which can exceed 1.
